LESSON 8 OF 106·Networking Fundamentals

How Data Moves: Packets and the Layered Stack

Why data is chopped into packets, how each layer of the stack wraps it in its own header, and how defenders use layer language to reason about traffic.

Beginner14 min
Why this matters

Networks move data as small labelled chunks called packets. Each layer of the network stack adds its own header, and each layer only needs to understand the layer above and below it. Security work is mostly about knowing which layer a control belongs to.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • When you send data, the application hands it to the transport layer, which adds ports so the right process receives it.
  • The network layer adds source and destination IP addresses and routes the packet hop by hop across the internet.
  • The data-link layer adds the hardware address for the next single hop, and is rewritten at every router.
  • Each layer provides a service to the layer above and relies on the layer below, which is why the stack is described as layered rather than monolithic.
  • Because headers are added and stripped as a packet travels, a device that only reads some layers can be fooled if a lower layer disagrees with a higher one.

The background

  • The layered design comes from the 1970s packet-switched experiments, which were built so that one part of the network could be replaced without redesigning the rest.
  • TCP/IP became the practical standard and was formalised in the 1980s, with the four-layer model most people are taught today.
  • The original design assumed a relatively cooperative network, which is why authentication and encryption were added to lower layers later.
  • Virtualisation and overlay networks made the layering more abstract without changing the basic model.

Real-world examples

  • A firewall that only understands layer 3 and 4 can be bypassed by traffic carried inside an allowed protocol on an allowed port.
  • Encrypted traffic that terminates at a trusted proxy becomes plain text again for everything behind it, so the proxy is a security boundary.
  • A slow page load is often a layer problem: DNS latency, a distant server, or a congested link, and each needs a different fix.

What to look for

  • Identify which layer a control operates at before deciding whether it can be bypassed.
  • Check whether a boundary inspects the innermost payload or only the outer header.
  • Remember that headers are not removed until the packet reaches its destination, so sensitive data in a header is exposed on every hop.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Log and alert at the layer where the threat actually appears, not only at the edge.
  • Treat any layer that terminates encryption as part of your trusted computing base.
  • Keep protocol filtering and inspection consistent so the layers cannot disagree about the same connection.
